power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Mental health inpatient wards can be unsettling places to be and there is evidence that engagement with a programme of activities on or off the wards can provide numerous benefits to patients.
However, there has been little research conducted into the views of patients with psychosis or ward staff on ward activities or in their role in promoting recovery.
The aim of this paper is to explore how activities on acute inpatient wards can promote recovery in people living with psychosis.

A mixed qualitative methods design consisting of phase i) a mapping exercise on 12 wards employing observations, interviews and use of routine ward data to inform the selection of wards in next phase, and phase ii) in-depth case studies on 7 wards across 3 hospitals using qualitative interviews and ethnographic observations.
The study was conducted across a large inner-city mental health Trust in England serving a diverse population.
Data collection ran from 29.05.2023 to 29.03.2024.
Data were analysed using framework method informed by the CHIME conceptual framework for personal recovery.
There was extensive lived experience involvement in the study.
Research ethics approval was obtained for the study and reporting follows the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR).
A total of 78 participants took part in the in-depth case studies, including patients with psychosis (n= 41), ward staff (n=28), community partners (n=6), and senior managers (n=3).

We present results of the framework analysis charted against the components of the CHIME framework: i) connectedness; ii) hope and optimism about the future; iii) identity; iv) meaning in life; and v) empowerment.
This study of activities on inpatient mental health wards for patients with psychosis focused on recovery, unlike most previous studies which tend to focus on boredom.
We recruited 41 patients diagnosed with psychosis currently on inpatient wards.

The recruitment and inclusion of this population is important as people with psychosis are frequently excluded from research studies, which may contribute to health care inequalities seen in this population.
The inclusion of people with lived experience in our research team perhaps aided this process, helping us establish trust with potential participants on the wards.
The findings indicate strong alignment with all elements of the CHIME recovery framework and provide explicit examples of how engagement in activities on wards can aid recovery.
Skilled facilitation and the involvement of people from wider community groups, including those with lived experience of mental illness and hospital use is valued.

Our recruitment of a substantial proportion of patients (and staff) from Black communities reflected the efforts of the research team and the demographics of the local population and perhaps the over-representation of Black patients on inner city mental health wards.
This study further emphasises the importance of activities in the experiences and recovery of patients with psychosis in otherwise restrictive environments.

This study shows that the provision of activities on wards can stimulate, motivate, aid and support the recovery of people with psychosis and help prepare them for discharge and re-connection with the wider community.
There has been surprisingly little definition or discussion of the role, function and design of acute inpatient mental healthcare.

An interview study with multidisciplinary staff found that patients were admitted because they appear likely to harm themselves or others, and because they are suffering from severe mental illness, and/or because they or their family/community require respite, and/or because they have insufficient support and supervision available to them .
The tasks of acute inpatient care are then to keep patients safe, assess their problems, treat their mental illness, meet their basic care needs, and provide physical healthcare.
These tasks are completed through 24-hour staff presence, containment, treatment provision, and complex organisation and management.

Later, Bowers et al., developed a conceptual model of inpatient care that identified the primary admission tasks may include any or all of assessment, treatment of acute illness, providing safe and highly tolerant accommodation, rehabilitation, and the resolution of personal distress.

text.text: However, patients also bring with them other life and health problems.
While not a cause of admission, these problems are also managed by inpatient staff and, where they can be resolved, represent an 'admission bonus'.
Inpatient wards are uniquely able to enforce treatment, provide regular observation to contain risks, and tolerate behaviour which would be unmanageable or unacceptable in the community.

Inpatient admission also offers respite from and space to address stressors in the person's home environment, and the potential, through 24-hour care, to provide high levels of interpersonal contact and therapeutic engagement, often through a range of ward activities .
In England, the importance of activities has been recognised in the new Culture of Care standards for mental health inpatient services.
Psychiatric inpatient care is most often unpopular -with both patients and many staffand can be traumatising, re-traumatising and coercive .

Tensions exist between keeping severely mentally distressed people safe whilst trying to build and sustain engaging, accepting, therapeutic relationships and milieu, often within health care systems and organisations that are inadequately funded and woefully understaffed.
Yet those staff that commit their time and energies to providing inpatient care often do so with great skill and humanity.
A cross-national comparative case study reported positive practice within acute inpatient wards, with evidence of safe, respectful, compassionate care.
Patients are at significant risk of relapse and suicide after discharge from inpatient care with lack of social connectedness likely to be a prime factor .

The National Confidential Inquiry into Suicide and Safety in Mental Health (2024) reported that 13% of all patient suicides were completed within 3 months of hospital discharge, with the highest number of deaths occurring within 48 hours post discharge.
This highlights the importance of providing patients in hospital with coping skills before discharge.
Providing effective care and support at these crucial times is of huge importance to patients, their families and mental health staff to maintain safety and stability following discharge.

Understanding activities and their value Bowers et al (2005) investigated and described the purpose and philosophy of inpatient mental healthcare and found, alongside the use of medication and therapeutic engagement by staff, a 'diverse and rather idiosyncratic range of psychosocial treatments on offer' (p.20).

text.text: Interspersed with these were a range of other organised or self-directed activities that may serve a range of purposes including minimising boredom, providing relaxation, promoting interaction, or maintaining physical health.
Such activities may include art, music, computer games, social media, gardening, exercise and discussion groups.
Evidence suggests engagement in activity is important and may be beneficial to patient outcomes.
The City128 study found that the provision of a comprehensive programme of activities was associated with lower rates of self-harm, reduced more serious selfharm and was highly valued by patients .
The provision of activities has also been linked with reduced levels of restraint , increased levels of recovery and improved patient experience.
Concern about the lack of activities on mental health inpatient wards, with a lack of therapeutic direction on the wards with little for patients to do, is long-standing .
Prior to this study, we published a systematic review of the literature on service users' views on ward activities .

Key findings included: • Boredom is a big issue on inpatient mental health wards that is linked to poor patient satisfaction, feelings of frustration and increased incidents of self-harm and aggression.
This is even more so for people detained under mental health legislation.
• Where wards have a good range of activities, for example art, music, computer games, gardening and exercise, patients felt less bored and had improved well-being.
• Over many years, studies have reported a lack of activities, especially during evenings and weekends.
Little is known about what activities service users want, or how activities might be meaningful for them.
• Few studies have asked patients about what activities would be useful and why.

The lack of activity provision and the boredom experienced by patients remains a prominent issue, as highlighted by a recent scoping review on boredom, meaningful activities and the occupational therapist's role on inpatient wards .
They concluded that research into new models need to be developed to address the persistent problem of boredom and its negative consequences.
It is important to ensure the therapeutic needs and priorities for inpatient care, including activities, are obtained from people with psychosis .

People with schizophrenia or other psychoses have the second highest number of admissions experiencing psychosis who are currently receiving care from an acute mental health inpatient ward using a mixed-methods Q-methodology approach.

Analysis revealed four distinct themes relating to factors that promote recovery in the acute mental health inpatient setting: i) stability, independence and 'keeping a roof over your head'; ii) hope, optimism and enhancing well-being; iii) personal change, self-management and social support; and iv) symptom reduction through mental health support.
They concluded that staff on acute mental health wards need to ensure that they are considering the personal recovery needs of inpatients.
Symptom reduction was valued by some, but broad psychosocial factors were also a priority.
Those with psychosis face additional barriers to accessing community activities that may benefit their recovery.
People living with psychosis are far more likely than other service users to experience stigma, discrimination, marginalisation within families, and exclusion from community organisations .
Black people and people of colour are disproportionately affected by racism and show increased rates of psychosis.

Furthermore, socio-economic inequalities and poor life skills of people experiencing psychosis are associated with higher rates of health-risk behaviours that are further exacerbated by illness factors such as lack of motivation or the adverse effects of medication.

It is therefore important that research exploring activities and their benefits to recovery consider patients who experience psychosis as they are often overlooked within research but are likely to benefit considerably from engaging with meaningful activities.
This paper reports from a wider study of ward activities for people with psychosis and focuses on how activities may support recovery.
The aim of this paper is to identify how activities on acute inpatient wards can promote recovery in people living with psychosis.
The Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) have been used to guide the reporting of the research (see S1).

We employed a mixed qualitative methods design consisting of phase i) a mapping exercise employing observations, interviews and use of routine ward data to inform the selection of wards in phase 2, and ii) in-depth case studies using qualitative interviews and ethnographic observations.
This study was conducted across a large inner-city mental health Trust in England serving a diverse population.
Phase 1 mapping took place across 12 wards on 3 hospital sites, and phase 2 on 7 wards across the same 3 hospital sites.
Data collection ran from 29.05.2023 to 29.03.2024.

The study sample consisted of patients identified by a clinician as having a diagnosis of psychosis, close to discharge and who met the inclusion criteria, and ward staff involved in providing activities (e.g., activities coordinators, occupational therapists), staff less directly involved in the provision of activities (e.g., mental health nurses, psychiatrists, ward managers), and community partners involved in the provision of activities for patients both on and off the ward.

Researchers approached ward managers to distribute information sheets to staff, who shared that information with patients.
Staff self-selected to participate in the study by liaising directly with the research team.

Patients meeting inclusion criteria and having capacity to consent were approached by ward staff who spoke with the patient about the study and provided them with a copy of the information sheet to consider.
If patients expressed an interest, a member of the research team approached the person to provide more information on the study and answer questions.

After initial contact with the research team, participants were given a 24-hour period to consider whether they wanted to participate before being invited for an interview when written informed consent was obtained.

A member of the research team (CR) facilitated a Lived Experience Advisory Panel (LEAP) recruited for this study, consisting of seven people with lived experience of inpatient mental healthcare, including four with psychosis and one a carer of someone with psychosis.
Members were of diverse ethnic backgrounds and included five women and two men.

The LEAP members contributed to the design of the study, defining activities, development of the interview schedule, practice interviews prior to data collection on the wards, supported recruitment of participants on the wards, assisted with patient interviews, and supported the analysis and interpretation of the data, taking part in coding sessions to identify themes in the interview transcripts.
The LEAP met once a month for two hours with researchers attending all meetings, presenting updates from each phase of the study, discussing findings and agreeing next steps.
Members were provided with training and paid for their time.

The core research team consisted of mental health nurse researchers with experience of inpatient wards (GB, AS), mental health researchers (CR, UF, ET), an occupational therapist researcher (JW) and a lived experience researcher (CC).
Regular team meetings took place throughout the study where developments and interim findings were discussed.
UF and AS had previously published on ward activities and GB had previously led a charity promoting and supporting ward activities.

To assist with our case study site selection of wards in which we would conduct indepth investigations, we mapped the current service provision on 12 acute inpatient wards across the three included hospital sites.
Our aim for this phase was to gather key information including:  Ward level details such as staffing levels, bed numbers, and average length of stay.
 Rates of incidents per ward, including rates of violence and aggression.

 Range of activities offered, who delivers activities, engagement with community partners to deliver activities, and facilities available on and off wards, e.g., green spaces, gym access, use of remote technologies, etc.
 Demographic overview of patients on the wards from the past month inclusive of patient ethnicity and diagnosis.
 Capacity of the ward to host researchers.

With the aid of a Trust Lived Experience Research Ambassador (SP), researcher CR made initial contact with nurse ward managers and occupational therapist (OT) leads to introduce the study and arranged a visit to each ward.
CR then attended ward meetings and OT leads meetings to widen engagement with ward-based staff and activity coordinators across the wards.

Prior to mapping, our team worked with LEAP members to develop a definition and examples of what is considered an activity and the types of activities they found meaningful to support engagement and discussion with people on the wards.
Members of the research team (CR, CC, GB) visited each of the 12 wards to conduct observations of daily ward life to obtain a sense of the activities taking place and engagement in these activities.

This included attending and observing the activities happening on and off the wards, discussing the timetable with ward staff to understand the activity provision, talking to patients to understand whether the timetable was consistent, shadowing ward staff to understand the ward context and environment, and visiting the facilities both on and off the ward for any activities provided by staff or community partners.
Data were captured via observation fieldnotes that were written and recorded during or immediately following these observation periods on the wards.
Details of the physical environment were recorded for each ward, including rooms available for activities and the general layout and size of the ward and rooms.
Staffing levels were recorded from officially reported staffing data.
Activities were recorded using a structured activity mapping tool, with engagement with patients being recorded using the Camden Staff-Patient Activity Record (CaSPAR).
Following the collection of data from each ward, CR created an anonymised matrix to display redacted information for all 12 wards.

The matrix included an overview of each ward using the Trust data and observational data, with accompanying graphs and charts summarising key elements alongside a traffic light system for each ward based on six criteria: 1.
Staffing fill rate (based on Trust provided data) 2.
Staff engagement with the project (based on researcher observations) 3.
Proportion of patients with a diagnosis of psychosis (based on anonymised routine data provided by the NHS Trust) 4.
Person centred approach (e.g., staff engaged with patients in activities, based on researcher observations) 5.
Provision of ward activities (based on timetables provided by ward staff during visits) 6.
Activities timetable followed (based on researcher observations)
This anonymised matrix of the wards was reviewed by the entire research team.
For each hospital site the team made a collective decision based on this data to ensure a range of wards were represented, with at least one male and one female ward being included per hospital site.

Decisions were made to ensure selection of wards that represented different approaches to activities including wards with good activities staff provision (e.g., an OT and activity coordinator employed on the ward) and wards with limited activities staff provision; wards with a structured timetable of activities versus wards with flexible and unstructured approaches to activities; wards that were delivering activities either in house or via community in-reach versus wards with limited or no community in-reach.
As a result, we were able to explore a range of experiences from staff and patients, and to ensure that the study accounts for the vast range of contexts of wards represented within this Trust.
From this process seven wards were selected for further in-depth case study investigation of activities.
In hospital A, two male wards and one female ward with high levels of patients with psychosis were selected.
These wards provided a diverse range of activities, selected to represent a "model ward", a ward with a limited activities timetable, and a ward with a strictly followed activities timetable.
In hospital B, one male and one female ward with high levels of psychosis were selected to represent a ward with high levels of activities, and a ward with limited activities.

In hospital C, one male and one female ward with high levels of psychosis were selected to represent a ward with limited activities and staffing, and a ward with a good range of activities and good staffing.
Case study method allows the exploration of a particular phenomenon within dynamic contexts where multiple influencing variables are difficult to isolate.
It allows consideration of historical and social contexts and is especially useful in explaining real- life links that may be too complex for survey or experimental approaches .

Within our case study design, each ward was defined as a 'case', and we used a mixed methods approach to triangulate data to provide a full picture of activity provision and experiences for each ward.

We employed semi-structured qualitative interviews to explore participants' experiences and views regarding the current provision of activities on the ward , their views on what activities should be provided by whom, when, where and how often; which activities are of most benefit or challenging for patients with psychosis; and the barriers and facilitators experienced when providing or taking part in activities provided on and off the ward.
This paper focuses on data around activities and recovery.
Example questions include: Q5.

Other studies have told us that there are certain things about activities that are helpful -I'm going to mention a few of these and talk about how important these are to you and what things might do these for you: Activities stop that people feeling bored -is this important to you?
What kinds of activities do you think do this?
Activities that build a sense of community -is this important to you?
What types of activities might do this?
Activities that support recovery -is that important to you?
What types of activities might do this?
Activities that promote wellbeing, including physical health -is this important to you?
What types of activities might do this?

We aimed to recruit 6 patients and 4 staff on each ward, plus at least one senior manager and two community partners providing input on each ward, providing a good range of views on each ward and a large total of participants.
Interviews were conducted by two health service researchers (CR, UF), a mental health nurse researcher
Additionally, the team (CR, GB, CC) conducted non-participant observations .

We focused on conducting observations during planned activities and at set times when service users were more likely to be engaged in self-directed activities to observe who engaged in which activities, how, where, when and why.

Data were captured via anonymised observation field notes that were written and recorded during or immediately following these observation periods on the wards to provide insights and understanding into the experiences of the researcher on the ward.
For interview and observation data, we conducted framework analysis informed by the CHIME framework of personal recovery.

The CHIME conceptual framework was developed from a systematic review and narrative synthesis on personal recovery in mental illness and identified five recovery processes comprising: i) connectedness; ii) hope and optimism about the future; iii) identity; iv) meaning in life; and v) empowerment (giving the acronym CHIME) .
Our coding framework used the five CHIME elements to record views and experiences of activities aligning to those aspects related to recovery using a deductive coding approach.

To ensure that the analysis captured other elements not aligned with the CHIME framework, a secondary inductive coding was conducted by the team to identify additional themes, which are reported elsewhere.
This initial stage was undertaken by three members of the study team with each researcher charting data summaries onto the framework for each of the interviews (CR, ET, GB).
These summaries were presented and discussed several times with members of the LEAP and the wider research team.

Findings from all areas of the study were presented and discussed at a consensus exercise attended by over 40 staff and patient participants towards the end of the study where priority topics for further work within the service were discussed.
These are reported elsewhere.

Many patients identified that making connections with other patients and staff on the ward can be a challenge.
There was a strongly shared sentiment amongst staff and patients that activities are one way of overcoming this challenge.
To create connections between patients, participating in activities and sharing resources were agreed to be an informal way to interact, break the ice, and enable bonding on the wards.
Connection on the ward between patients was frequently emphasised as beneficial for multiple reasons.
It can reduce isolation and distract from (41 ) negative thoughts by creating a space where patients can share and understand their experiences.

text.text: We all have quite a few things in common.
We're all women that have been through the mental health system and stuff like that.
So, we already have that.
I feel like that's one of the first things that people get a bit worried about, disclosing mental health.
If we're all here, we know we've got some form of an issue, so that's the ice already completely gone. (c20, patient, female)
Staff and patients recognised that group activities where the patient's experience is discussed creates a safe space to get to know each other and form understandings of one another.
Staff noted that this can lead to greater empathy between patients and creates a space for informal mutual or peer support.
Staff also noted that sharing interests through activities can allow for patients to move beyond their differences, for example, age differences.

When you've got a big group of you and you're all being positive together and me and the activity co-ordinator are facilitating the positive side of things, then actually, being able to talk to each other, it brings them out of their shell really. (a13, staff, female)
Many staff and patients indicated that involvement in activities resulted in trust and friendship building between patients.
This was reported to improve the sense of community on the ward and was important for reducing tensions and negative interactions that can lead to violence and aggression.

I think definitely to build a sense of community, because if you are reaching out to your fellow patients and the patients are reaching out to you, and you get to know them on first-name terms, [it is] far less likely for there to be fractious interactions with each other.
I think you're much more likely to talk to someone in a much more calm and sedate manner. (b16, patient, male)

A divergence in views was noted when one staff member acknowledged that relationships between patients can sometimes be unhelpful for some patients' recovery while another two staff members stated that some patients prefer not to connect with others on the wards and find group activities challenging.
And I think it can go one of two ways, you know.
I think sometimes...
Obviously we don't want them to depend too much on each other because, as I said, they're all in here for their own reasons. (a13, staff, female)

Aligning with this, a few patients rejected the idea of connection on the ward as helpful to their recovery as they were being cautious of others in relation to safety concerns, disingenuous relationships and high turnover of patients, which lead to a lack of motivation to engage with others and group activities.
What's the point in doing community activities to get to know each other, then all of a sudden you've got to go?
That's causing a relationship breakdown and that's one of the things that's making us mentally unwell.
Rejection, and having a sense of nothing. (a28, patient, non-binary)
Many patients also noted that activities allow for a space to break down barriers between staff and patients and create a connection between the two.
Activities can help interactions with staff by improving communication in an informal setting that allows staff and patients to get to know each other.
Staff also suggested that activities can be beneficial for patient-staff relationships.
When we play football with the staff and the patients it's really good.
Playing sports in that way means you get to be friendly with people you wouldn't normally and breaks down a bit of that barrier, so you get to see the staff better. (b14, patient, male)

There's been Zumba classes, or sessions on the ward and staff will get into that.... there's something about that kind of community cohesion on a ward that breaks down people's professions and hierarchy and everybody's doing the same thing.
That's definitely helped staff and patients to get better and share something on an equal level with them.
It's not teaching this thing, it's just all learning at the same time. (c23, manager: staff, female)
Activities coordinators were identified by patients as staff with a good relationship with patients due to their interactions with patients during activities.
Patients emphasised that having good facilitators, especially those with lived experience and external facilitators, can create a positive connection and trust.
Volunteers help as well because they're in between staff and a patient.
Usually they have lived experience, so it makes it a little bit less awkward because they can engage with it, act silly and that will bring people out of their shells.
We had volunteers on the old ward, and they helped bridge the gap sometimes. (b11, patient, female)
It was recognised by staff that having groups where staff attend or where patients and staff run them together, provided the potential to break down barriers and level the power dynamics.
A need for staff to get involved and be open and willing to share with patients was also highlighted to improve connection.
And there's one of the interventions -'get to know me' -which is about staff and patients getting to know each other, and they'll build up that rapport.
But I think that is so powerful....
And they appreciate it.
Because I know so much about them (b1, staff, female)
Patients and staff often described activities as beneficial for creating hope and optimism for many patients.
Interviewees found that activities create a space for patients to think positively and value efforts.
Several patients mentioned that activities are enjoyable and create a positive mindset as they are something to look forward to, they can provide respite from the ward and lift the mood on the ward.
Patients also valued the facilitators' efforts and the opportunities when they arose for skills development.

I like going for a walk, or the pottery is something to look forward to. (c20, patient, female) I mean, for me, again, activities helping recovery, when I did the Music sessions, I found that beneficial.
And, like I said, with my leave, when I go and I do my activities, in the gym, and that sort of stuff, I find it's a nice little respite. (a31, patient, male)
Echoing the above, staff acknowledged that activities also create positive feelings during and after sessions, with activities able to recharge the patients' spirits.
Having at least one activity a day for these patients, I think it's so important to be able to have something to look forward to in the day.
And knowing that you've got something to look forward to, as well.
Otherwise, you know, some of our patients come in with depression, things like that.

So that hopelessness that they're feeling is just reiterated if there is nothing for them to do, nothing to engage them in, nothing to support them, to try and find new hobbies or anything like that. (a13, staff, female)

Staff recognised the importance of having something to look forward to that can distract from negative thinking and possibly shift the patient's perspective of their time in the hospital to a more positive experience, thereby supporting hope and engagement in their recovery.
Staff noted that patients particularly valued garden breaks or time away from the ward and grooming activities for lifting their mood.
Activities might help them to see that it's beneficial to come to hospital.
Because sometimes we are restricting these patients to come to hospital, so we should be able to make some provision for them, to engage them.
Because if they were at home, they would be engaging themselves.
So just to make them feel it's...
Not to regret coming to hospital in the first place. (a24, staff, female) If they're unwell for a while, or they don't have someone who can take them, then it just makes them feel a bit rubbish.
So, then [name] will do their hair and then they feel nice after.
It does make people feel better. (c15, staff, female)
Some patients recognised activities as showing patients that there is hope for recovery and the future with some activities helping them find and build a path forward.

The one [activity] about the story, like story of your life, the tree of life group, when are thinking about, trying to chat about what is going on and just think about your life, what is your path, stuff like that.

You can just have a chance to think about it again and think through and like, "Oh yes." (a21, patient, sex not provided) When you are transitioning from that dark point, coming back to myself, the activities are going to help to keep you engaged on something else. (a29, patient, female)
Staff frequently noted that activities can provide hope for recovery and aspirations for the future and a space to plan.
They recognised the importance of activities for providing a sense of purpose and achievement, often through the creation of something.
Some patients' hopes for the future included a desire to volunteer, work or study, which some activities could help develop the skills for.
Patients often wished to continue activities in the community but expressed the need for signposting to relevant community groups.
Staff also recognised the need to encourage patients to continue activities in the community when discharged.
Activities can help patients tap into their potential, reconnect with past interests and provide them with the hope that they can do things that can make them feel better.

A few patients noted that activities created motivation to want to change by keeping them focused and on track for recovery, which was seen as achievable through helping change negative thought patterns and building confidence.

is your thoughts that break down, you start not doing things properly, end up doing the wrong thing because of the thoughts in your head where if you are doing something you focus on it doesn't affect you as much.

Like cooking or cleaning it doesn't confuse your head as much as you have something else to do. (a3, patient, male) I'd never painted before and things like that, so I was trying new things in the hospital.
I think that gave me the confidence to think, "Maybe I can do this when I leave."
I realised I like lots of different things. (b10, patient, female)
Patients also found that activities could be a source of hope inspiring relationships for some.
Activities with lived experience volunteers had the potential to inspire patients, as hearing about other people's success fostered hope and a belief in recovery.
When I saw the volunteers that have lived a life after the hospital it made it seem more real that there's life outside and it's going to be fine. (b10, patient, female)
A handful of patients recognised the role that activities played in providing a positive sense of identity.
Activities achieved this by allowing for reconnection with previous interests which provided a sense of normality or feeling like themselves again and reminded the patient of happier times.
Trying new activities assisted with a positive sense of identity as it provided a source of confidence for patients.
The thing I noticed with activities is people with identity issues, that I've suffered with myself, is it brings you back together.
It makes you a whole person.

You're building yourself. (a8, patient, male) Having the opportunity through activities to reconnect with one's body was noted by one patient as important for a positive sense of self, another patient noted that when you are on the ward there is a disconnect from self as you can look different which negatively impacts identity.
Yoga was a lot of slow movement, just calming down.
A lot of calming down for anxiety if you're feeling distressed.
Just stretching and stuff like that.
I think that did help me a lot to come back to myself a little bit.
I started to take it more seriously that I shouldn't just sit in one spot all day, not stretch and not move.
Connect a little bit more with my body.

We all thought it was a bit hippy, but it did make me feel happier. (b10, patient, female) It's really difficult when you have to come to terms with the fact that you don't look like how you usually present.... one thing that you've lost is whatever you would present yourself as, based on makeup or hair or whatever maintenance and stuff. (c20, patient, female)
Activities were also identified by some patients as helping with regaining a positive sense of identity through tackling stigma.
This was achieved by providing a space to discuss and make sense of their diagnosis with others.
It takes the stigma out of it.
A lot of people still stigmatise, at least we can laugh about it, that's helpful. (b15, patient, female)

Staff also acknowledged that activities could allow for a reconnection with something the patient enjoys, a sense of accomplishment, expression of creativity and reconnection with one's body, which is all recognised as contributing to a positive sense of self.
Community support and social connection also were noted as helpful for regaining a positive sense of self.
I think a lot of the activities there can be a sense of achievement, there can be a better sense of self, there can be interpersonal connections.
I think there are so many things that doing these activities bring about and they are helpful for wellbeing. (c1, staff, female)
Activities for some patients are helpful for giving meaning to their mental health experience.

Patients highlighted the need to provide a space to share their experiences and diagnosis with other patients or staff, with it being noted that there is often limited time on the ward to do this or limited information provided to assist with understanding their diagnosis and experiences.

But psychosis effects everyone different, some people see that someone is after them, or something else, activities is actually going out there and talking to them about what their symptoms are and what they are going through.
So maybe having a group where you can sit and discuss your psychosis.
It affects everyone very differently. (a3, patient, male)

Staff also recognised the need to provide a space through activities for patients to share about their experiences and discuss their diagnosis, which some suggested could be achieved through creative outlets or discussion groups with other patients.
think a chance to express feelings, challenging emotions in different art forms, different activities, different spaces, I think is really important.
That chance to recover in different ways. (c21, community staff, female)

To assist with recovery, patients and staff identified the need to discuss personal visions for wellness, to understand recovery in their own terms, and work with their diagnosis rather than against it.
Patients identified activities as helpful for focusing and understanding their mind and some activities helped with grounding and accepting their circumstances and even limitations.
But I feel like, instead of that, it's like we need to find a way for people to work with what they've got because some things can't be changed.
So, the best thing we can do for them is to allow them to be free and help them to be the best version of what they have and what they're dealing with. (a8, patient, male)
In terms of activities, like I say, play, imagination.

I would say if people are experiencing hallucinations or delusions, then not necessarily going fully into that with them but maybe stepping in, just slightly and almost validating that, because they're experiencing that as a truth, so almost validating that but not getting sucked right into it.
Just working with that within the arts therapy rather than being scared and shying away from it, I think, yes, it is really important. (c1, staff, female)

Numerous staff and patients indicated activities as helpful for building a meaningful life which consisted of having access to education and employment supports, giving responsibility (e.g., caring for a plant) and providing skills for independent living so they can have a positive social role when discharged.

When patients are discharged, if they could be encouraged to participate in work, kind of a job to do, if you are idle, most people are idle they turn to substance misuses, if when they are discharged and they have nothing to do what do they do?
(a5, staff, female)
He has no support network.

So being involved in something like a Men's Shed would really give him a sense of purpose, a sense of routine, a sense of community connection (b1, staff, female) Links to community resources on discharge also help with achieving goals for a meaningful life.

Other activities that consist of long-term projects and provide a sense of purpose and achievement were identified as helpful for a meaningful life, as were activities that involve the patients in running them and activities that are meaningful to the patients rather than based on assumptions.
When trying to find meaning in their experience some patients identified faith and spirituality as helpful for creating a safe space and understanding of self and their mental health.
These patients noted that wards need to facilitate patients to practice different faiths, spiritual beliefs, and multiple cultural activities.
So, the priest put me at ease and things started to go right.
So, it's a positive thing.
It can be useful sometimes.
But I think there should be not just a priest, there should be someone coming in for all different faiths. (a8, patient, male)
Staff also identified faith and spirituality as helpful for creating a safe space and understanding of oneself and experiences.
Staff and patients identified activities as helping patients focus on and realise their strengths.
Activities can provide a space where patients can try new things and develop new skills or tap into old interests to build existing skills.
Focusing on strengths can help patients gain confidence, self-esteem and self-worth.
Meaningful activities that have an end product or provide a sense of accomplishment and when run by good facilitators, including those with lived experience, assist this.
And it is important for them to feel like you don't have to be good at this, just do it because you're trying to express yourself.
And then once people do that, they realise, "Oh, I'm actually not bad at this," and that's instilling their confidence. (a8, patient, male)
In preparation for discharge, providing employment and educational support is recognised by staff and patients as important for equipping people to take control.
They also recognised that to take personal responsibility when discharged there needs to be activities that provide independent living skills for patients.
And I would love to have a kitchen on our ward, for example.
Because I think in terms of allowing these ladies to keep that independence and for them to be able to get skills that they don't necessarily have.
Or keep the skills that they've got. (a13, staff, female) Yeah, skills stuff, as well.
Just, like, learning stuff.
Basic things, like learning how to cook would be useful, very useful, for just in general with life. (c14, patient, male)
Two patients furthered this by highlighting that relapse prevention and drug education was also needed to support them to feel empowered and in control of their lives once discharged.
If you don't have relapse prevention mechanisms or activities or things, people don't know how to get out of the same rut. (c8, patient, male)
Involving patients in running activities and giving space for them to have control or freedom within the activity is identified by staff and patients as helpful for empowering patients.
Staff further noted that activities provide a space to celebrate patients' wins and foster hope for the future.
And I think there would be more people who would be open to leading activities, if they were asked, and they felt they would be supported in doing it. (b15, patient, female)

Staff identified ownership over the activity, for example, the community meeting or by donating as a form of payment for a sports activity, and ownership over the ward environment, for example, allowing patients to decorate it, as a source of control and responsibility for patients.
I'm trying to empower patients to have their voice and to advocate for the ward what we need.
And although the community meeting is very challenging and very draining to facilitate, when it's just you facilitating it, it's so important.
Because it gives them that space, that open space, to discuss their concerns and build that sense of community. (b1, staff, female)

A considerable proportion of staff and a few patients acknowledge activities as helpful for patients to take back control of their lives as they figure out what makes them feel better and can provide coping strategies to manage their illness.
This is the mantra I give to the guys.
I say that "I don't give you anything."
I said, "You've got all the power you have within you to fix yourself.

You've just got to learn to tap into that, and your body will help you." (a23, community staff, male) We used to have a psychologist that would come and do a joint group...we used to have that every week....
And the ladies really enjoyed it because it sort of gave them… It was called 'my life beyond the ward' or something.
And we'd talk about different skills that they could use, again 'managing emotions', and things like that. (a13, staff, female)
Staff and patients highlighted the importance of signposting to the community and finding groups that equip people to continue activities and take control of their lives when discharged.
Staff and patients also mentioned that some activities need to provide advocacy support and information about their rights to encourage patients to take control of their situations.
Just understanding, just being more clear about your rights, when it comes to the legal stuff....
So you don't feel like you don't have a voice, or you don't feel left out.

So advocacy things, stuff like that. (c14, patient, male) Discussion This study of activities on inpatient mental health wards for patients with psychosis focused on activities and recovery, which is unlike most previous studies of ward activities which tend to focus on boredom .
We recruited 41 patients diagnosed with psychosis currently on inpatient wards.

The recruitment and inclusion of this population is important as people with psychosis are frequently excluded from research studies , which may contribute to health care inequalities seen in this population .
Common reasons for excluding this patient group include concerns about the atient's capacity to provide informed consent, and the potential for high-risk adverse events and safety issues.
These concerns may reflect a misunderstanding of the nature of psychosis and perhaps an element of stigma towards this patient group.
A previous study reported that about two-thirds of patients with psychotic disorders questioned were willing to be contacted about participation in research .
In this study, even during inpatient admissions, we were able to obtain informed consent and conduct detailed interviews where patients described their experiences and views.
The inclusion of people with lived experience in our research team perhaps aided this process, helping us establish trust with potential participants on the wards .

The meaning in those experiences and start to map out a meaningful life and to wish for support in connecting or re-connecting with families, communities and organisations that can help their recovery.
The importance of support at this crucial stage was highlighted.
Some found help in faith or a spiritual dimension, but this was possibly under-explored in the interviews.
Finally, patients experienced empowerment by learning to take on more responsibility for themselves within and through the activities, with some co-leading activities.
Building skills, strengths and confidence in preparation for discharge were seen as important aspects of ward activities that need to be nurtured and supported at and beyond discharge.
Skilled facilitation and the involvement of people from wider community groups, including those with lived experience of mental illness and hospital use is valued.

This indicates the importance of ensuring wards can employ experienced occupational therapists and activities coordinators, while also finding ways to support the involvement of community organisations that may bring helpful activities onto the wards while also helping build connections that can be maintained and nurtured once the person leaves the ward.
These human, social connections are essential in helping maintain recovery and avoid relapse, re-admission or worse.

Hearing the voices of people with lived experience who are in recovery also shows the value of involving peer workers in ward activities and supporting people through and beyond the transition to community living.
The clear desire of most patients with psychosis interviewed to connect with, get to know and develop closer relationships with other patients and staff is important.

The closer relationships and recognition of shared experiences reduce the fear and anxiety (47, 48 ) frequently reported on mental health wards and can reduce the risk of tensions which too often lead to aggression, self-harm or absconding.

text.text: Acute mental health wards can be challenging settings not always conducive to recovery, yet participants spoke of activities providing something more positive and hopeful in environments characterised by containment and risk management.

People with psychosis admitted to inpatient wards may well be struggling with an illness that can shatter a clear understanding of self and others, with resulting raised levels of anxiety and suspicion.
They and other patients feel vulnerable and are often subject to the same stigmatising views of psychiatric hospitals and patients prevalent in wider society.

Similarly, helping patients and staff to see the individual person and to share moments of light relief and connection can help build therapeutic relationships and ward cultures that are conducive to positive experiences and outcomes, including recovery .

Such approaches echo the 'Knowing Each Other' intervention in the successful Safewards model designed to reduce conflict and containment on wards and are most beneficial when all staff are encouraged to contribute .
However, we must be mindful of the smaller number of people interviewed who remained cautious and less keen on closer relationships with others on the wards through activities.

We need to work with sensitivity to recognise that for various reasons, including awareness of the oftenfleeting connections made on wards, and previous experiences of trauma and/or neurodivergence, other approaches and options may be desirable to provide personcentred, trauma-informed care.
We successfully recruited 41

The importance of activities in providing safe effective inpatient care has been recognised in key national policy reports and this study further emphasises the importance of activities in the experiences and recovery of patients with psychosis in otherwise restrictive environments.

The findings also demonstrate that the provision of activities on wards can stimulate, motivate, aid and support the recovery of people with psychosis and help prepare them for discharge and re-connection with the wider community.

Building and maintaining connections with external agencies is essential and the active involvement of people with lived experience who can draw on their mutual experiences and act as role models is desirable.

Participants were invited to take part in an interview within a private space on the ward.
Interviews were scheduled for one hour with an additional 15 minutes before and after to obtain informed consent and answer any questions.
Participation was voluntary with participants free to withdraw at any time.
Patients were offered a £10 voucher following the interview.
Interviews were audio-recorded (except one, where detailed notes were taken) and saved to an encrypted server.
Interview recordings were transcribed by an external company, and the research team checked the transcripts for accuracy and pseudonymised all text.
All transcripts were allocated a unique ID number and imported to NVivo Version 14 for analysis.

The posters contained information on the study, on what the researcher would be observing on the ward, and names and photos of the researchers who would be attending the ward to conduct this work.
The information on the poster asked patients who objected to being observed to inform the clinical team or the researcher of this, and their data would not be included in the study.

As these activities collected no personal information or data directly related to any single individual and thus no single ward staff member or patient could be identified, we were not required to seek written consent from patients or staff present on the ward when observations were conducted in line with the NHS research ethics approval and the Medical Research Council's guidelines.

Access to the wards, staff and patients was aided by a Lived Experience Research Ambassador (SP), and a person with lived experience of inpatient care (CC) helped engage and recruit patients and conducted some of the patient interviews.

Similarly, the involvement of a mental health nurse researcher with extensive experience of working with people with psychosis (GB) aided the process, providing advice and support to the research team.The findings indicate strong alignment with all elements of the CHIME recovery framework and provide explicit examples of how engagement in activities on wards can aid recovery.
Engagement with activities helps break down barriers and potential tensions with other patients and staff through greater connection and providing opportunities to see the person beyond the labels.
Participants also spoke of activities helping create positive thinking and feelings at a time and in an environment that can feel frightening and suffocating.
Patients spoke of starting to develop hope and optimism for the future and stimulating a motivation to change.
Patients also described activities helping them discover their self, or to re-discover their identity, that had often been lost in the confusion and distress of mental illness.

Some spoke of re-connecting through physical activities with their physical bodies, that had been affected by periods of neglect during their illness and/or the effects of stifled motivation, lack of exercise and medication effects.
Activities also provide safe spaces to share and explore experiences of mental illness, of psychosis, of being on a mental health ward and of the stigma associated with mental illness.
Some were able to find patients with psychosis on inpatient wards and successfully interviewed 40 of those, alongside a similar number of staff.

People with psychosis are often excluded from research studies with implications for our understanding of such patients' experiences and a better recognition of what is required to ensure our services meet the needs of people with psychosis.

Our recruitment of a substantial proportion of patients (and staff) from Black communities reflected the efforts of the research team and the demographics of the local population and perhaps the over-representation of Black patients on inner city mental health wards.

However, our interviews did not include specific questions focused on race, ethnicity or health inequalities and perhaps as a result our analysis did not identify any specific issues of importance to this population.
The study took part within one NHS mental health service provider organisation, which may not be representative of other hospital settings thereby potentially limiting transferability of findings.
